449.title: The dog-duty ascetic
449.hook: a man living like a dog asks his fate; deeds bear fruit like themselves
449.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching on karma holds that intentional actions shape the one who does them, here and in future lives; some teachers use MN 57's four kinds of action to explain this, and stress that a person can change direction by practicing what is bright.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Upali the householder, and your line, keep giving to them. Did you keep one old kindness going? Day four hundred forty-nine.

In the Buddha's India, some ascetics took vows to live like animals, believing it would purify them and lead to heaven. Two such men come to the Buddha together. Punna has vowed to live like an ox. Seniya, naked, has vowed to live like a dog: he eats only food thrown on the ground, and when he sits down near the Buddha he curls up like a dog. Punna asks the Buddha a direct question: this man has kept the dog vow a long time. Where will he go after death? Today: the dog-duty ascetic.
screen: `ASCETICS WHO LIVED LIKE ANIMALS.` → `PUNNA THE OX, SENIYA THE DOG.` → `WHERE WILL HE GO AFTER DEATH?`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-seventh discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the dog-duty ascetic. The Buddha refuses to answer. Enough, Punna, let it be. Don't ask me that. Punna asks again. Again the Buddha declines. Only on the third request does he answer, and his answer is careful. If someone develops the dog habit fully, the dog mind, the dog manner, then after death, he says, they are reborn among dogs. And if they hold the view that this will take them to heaven, that is a wrong view, and a wrong view leads to a bad destination. The same with the ox vow. Hearing this, Seniya weeps. Not, he says, because of what the Buddha said, but because he has practiced this vow for so long. Then the Buddha teaches the principle beneath it. There are four kinds of action. Dark action with dark results. Bright action with bright results. Mixed action with mixed results. And action that is neither dark nor bright, which leads to the end of action itself. Deeds bear fruit like themselves. A being, the Buddha says, is reborn according to what they have done; they become what they practice. And here's the gentle ending. Both men take refuge. Seniya asks to go forth, trains, and in time, the text says, becomes one of the awakened. The man who practiced being a dog for so long practiced something else, and became that instead. The hard answer and the hopeful ending are the same teaching: what we keep doing, we become.
screen: `THE BUDDHA DECLINES, TWICE` · `DOG HABIT, DOG MIND, AMONG DOGS` · `FOUR KINDS OF ACTION, DARK TO BRIGHT` · `SENIYA TRAINS AND AWAKENS` · then, large: `YOU BECOME THE HABIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see one habit's shape. Sit, and choose one thing you do almost every day: how you wake, how you answer the phone, how you speak to yourself in the mirror. Picture it clearly. Then ask, without blame: if I practiced this for ten more years, what would I become? Let the answer come honestly. If it's good, rest in it. If not, picture one bright action to practice instead. Then breathe. The bell holds the time.
The dog-duty ascetic. Seniya, who lived like a dog for a long time, heard that deeds bear fruit like themselves, and then practiced his way to awakening. Today's word.
Your line: you become the habit. Today, catch one small habit as it happens, and ask what it's practicing you into. Day four hundred forty-nine.

match.prompt: the four kinds of action — tap the pairs.
pairs: leads to the end of action

myth: the Buddha answered Punna's question right away
he declined twice, and answered only on the third request.
Seniya wept because the Buddha's words were harsh
he said he wept because he had practiced the dog vow so long.
Seniya later went forth and became one of the awakened
the text says he trained and in time reached the goal.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a man asks where his friend, who has lived like a dog for years, will go after death. the answer is painful. what do you do the first time he asks?
options: answer bluntly.
decline: let it be, don't ask me that.
promise his friend heaven.
fork.reveal: the Buddha declines twice. only when asked a third time does he answer, carefully, and then teaches the four kinds of action.

original.note: Pali kukkura: dog. the discourse is the Kukkuravatika Sutta, the dog-duty ascetic.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma is a judge handing out punishments.
what it means: deeds bear fruit like themselves; we become what we practice, and can practice something else.

what a scholar hears: MN 57's fourfold scheme of dark, bright, mixed and neither-dark-nor-bright action also appears in the Anguttara Nikaya; the fourth kind is the intention to abandon the other three.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 57, Kukkuravatika Sutta (the dog-duty ascetic)

450.title: The trap question
450.hook: Prince Abhaya brings a two-horned question; the answer depends on truth, benefit and timing
450.howItsDone: Buddhists study MN 58 as a guide to right speech: say only what is true and beneficial, and choose the right time, whether or not it is welcome; some teachers summarize it as checking truth, benefit and timing before speaking.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dog-duty ascetic, and your line, you become the habit. Did you catch one habit and ask what it's practicing you into? Day four hundred fifty.

Have you stopped wasting your money? Yes or no. Either answer sinks you. The sutta calls this kind of question two-horned: whichever way you answer, a horn catches you. Prince Abhaya is handed one by a rival teacher and sent to try it on the Buddha. The question, the teacher promises, will stick in the Buddha's throat like an iron hook: he can neither swallow it nor spit it out. If you can make him answer, he's told, people will say Abhaya refuted the great Gotama. Today: the trap question.
screen: `HAVE YOU STOPPED WASTING MONEY?` → `A TWO-HORNED QUESTION.` → `PRINCE ABHAYA TRIES IT.`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-eighth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse to Prince Abhaya. The question is: would the Buddha ever say something unwelcome, something that hurts another person? If he says yes, then how is he different from an ordinary person who hurts people? If he says no, then why did he say of his cousin Devadatta that he was headed for ruin, which made Devadatta furious? Abhaya asks. And the Buddha says: there's no one-sided answer to that. Abhaya says the plan has already failed, and confesses the whole plot. Now, Abhaya happens to have a baby boy sitting on his lap. So the Buddha asks: if this child, while you weren't looking, put a stick or a pebble in his mouth, what would you do? I'd take it out, Abhaya says. If I couldn't get it right away, I'd hold his head with one hand and hook it out with a finger of the other, even if it drew blood. Why? Out of compassion for the child. Just so, the Buddha says. Then he lays out how he speaks. If something is untrue, or true but not beneficial, he doesn't say it, welcome or not. If it is true and beneficial, he knows the right time to say it, whether it's welcome or unwelcome. Three questions: is it true? Is it beneficial? Is this the time? Sometimes a true, helpful word stings, like a finger in a baby's mouth, and the Buddha says it anyway, out of compassion. And a true word that wouldn't help, he leaves unsaid. The trap had two horns. The Buddha answered with three questions.
screen: `WOULD YOU EVER SAY WHAT HURTS?` · `NO ONE-SIDED ANSWER` · `A PEBBLE IN A BABY'S MOUTH` · `TRUE? BENEFICIAL? THE RIGHT TIME?` · then, large: `TRUTH, BENEFIT, TIMING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer one hard question simply. Think of something you've been asked, or need to say, that feels tricky: a hard truth for a friend, an honest answer at work. Sit, and run the three questions. Is it true? Is it helpful? Is now the time? Let each answer settle before the next. If all three are yes, picture saying it, plainly and kindly. If not, let it wait. Then rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
The trap question. A two-horned riddle meant to catch the Buddha, answered with a baby, a pebble, and three tests for speech. Today's word.
Your line: truth, benefit, timing. Today, before one hard sentence leaves your mouth, check all three. Day four hundred fifty.

myth: the Buddha never says anything unwelcome
if something is true and beneficial, he says it at the right time, welcome or not.
the Buddha used the baby on Abhaya's lap to answer
a father would hook a pebble from his child's mouth even if it drew blood, out of compassion.
anything true should be said at once
true but not beneficial isn't said; true and beneficial waits for the right time.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a prince asks: would you ever say something that hurts someone? yes seems to make you ordinary; no seems to contradict what you told Devadatta. what do you say?
options: yes.
no.
there's no one-sided answer to that.
fork.reveal: the Buddha refuses both horns, then uses the baby on Abhaya's lap to show that truth, benefit and timing decide what he says.

trapdoor: what you thought: kind speech means only saying nice things.
what it means: kind speech is true, beneficial and well-timed, even when it stings.
what a scholar hears: MN 58 sorts speech into six cases by true or untrue, beneficial or not, welcome or not; the Buddha speaks only in the two that are true and beneficial, at the proper time.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhayarajakumara Sutta (the discourse to Prince Abhaya)

451.title: How many feelings?
451.hook: two, three, five, six, eighteen, a hundred and eight: each count is a way of teaching
451.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers point to MN 59 to explain why the scriptures list things in different numbers (two, three or a hundred and eight kinds of feeling) and to encourage harmony when people describe the teaching in different ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the trap question, and your line, truth, benefit, timing. Before one hard sentence, did you check all three? Day four hundred fifty-one.

Two friends are arguing over how many seasons a year has. One says four: spring, summer, fall, winter. The other grew up where the year runs wet, then dry, and says two. Nobody is lying. They're counting the same year for different reasons. A carpenter named Pancakanga and a monk named Udayi once got stuck in exactly this kind of argument, about feelings. Neither would budge, and each was quoting the Buddha. Today: how many feelings?
screen: `FOUR SEASONS, OR TWO?` → `NOBODY IS LYING.` → `A CARPENTER AND A MONK, STUCK.`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-ninth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse on many kinds of feeling. Pancakanga, a royal carpenter, asks the monk Udayi: how many feelings did the Buddha teach? Three, says Udayi: pleasant, painful and neither. No, says Pancakanga, two: pleasant and painful. The neutral one, he says, the Buddha counts as a refined kind of pleasure. Three, says Udayi. Two, says Pancakanga. Ananda overhears and tells the Buddha. And the Buddha says: Ananda, Udayi's way was correct, and Pancakanga didn't accept it. Pancakanga's way was correct, and Udayi didn't accept it. Then he explains. I've taught two kinds of feeling in one way, three in another, five in another, six, eighteen, thirty-six, and a hundred and eight. Each count is a way of teaching, a lens for a purpose. And then he gives the warning. When people don't accept what has been well said in another way, you can expect them to quarrel and wound each other with verbal daggers. When they do accept it, you can expect them to live together like milk and water, looking at each other with kind eyes. You've heard both of those pictures before on this path: the daggers of Kosambi and the friends in the Gosinga wood. Here they meet. Then the discourse goes on to a ladder of happiness, from the pleasure of the senses, to the quieter joys of meditation, each one finer than the one before. So two people can be right about the same thing and still fight, because they're counting differently. Ask what someone is counting for before deciding they're wrong.
screen: `THREE FEELINGS, SAYS UDAYI; TWO, SAYS HE` · `BOTH WERE CORRECT` · `TWO, THREE, FIVE ... A HUNDRED AND EIGHT` · `DAGGERS, OR MILK AND WATER` · then, large: `MANY WAYS TO COUNT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count feelings two ways. Sit, and notice what you feel right now. First count it Udayi's way: is it pleasant, painful, or neither? Then count it Pancakanga's way: only pleasant or painful. Where does the neutral feeling go? Notice how the same moment looks a little different through each lens. Neither is wrong. Then let counting go, and just feel. The bell holds the time.
How many feelings? Two, three, five, six, eighteen, thirty-six, a hundred and eight: each one a way the Buddha taught, each true for its purpose. Today's word.
Your line: many ways to count. Today, when you disagree with someone, ask what they're counting for before you decide one of you is wrong. Day four hundred fifty-one.

he said both ways were correct; each simply didn't accept the other's.
the Buddha taught feelings in counts as high as a hundred and eight
two, three, five, six, eighteen, thirty-six, a hundred and eight: each a way of teaching.
the neutral feeling disappears in Pancakanga's count
he counts it as a refined kind of pleasure, within the two.

fork.setup: two of your students argue: one says you taught three kinds of feeling, the other says two. both have heard you say it. you're the Buddha. what do you say?
options: the one who said three is right.
both are correct; I've taught it many ways.
stop arguing and stop counting.
fork.reveal: the Buddha says both were correct, lists many counts, and warns that refusing another's well-spoken way leads to verbal daggers.

original.note: Pali vedana: feeling, the pleasant, painful or neither tone of experience.

trapdoor: what you thought: one of them must have been wrong.
what it means: the same truth can be counted many ways, each for a purpose; refusing the other's way is what starts the fight.
what a scholar hears: the count of a hundred and eight feelings (thirty-six in each of past, present and future) is one explanation some Buddhists give for the 108 beads on a mala; there are others.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 59, Bahuvedaniya Sutta (the many kinds of feeling)

452.title: The safe bet
452.hook: live as though actions have results; you lose nothing either way
452.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers use this sutta when talking with people who doubt rebirth: the advice to keep the precepts and act carefully stands either way, so it can be practiced before the big questions are settled.

segments.voice: Yesterday: how many feelings? Two, three, five, a hundred and eight. Your line was many ways to count. Did you count one feeling two different ways? Day four hundred fifty-two.

A village called Sālā, in the kingdom of Kosala. Its people have heard a lot of traveling teachers. One says there is another world after this one. Another says there isn't, and that nothing you do carries forward. Each one is very sure. Then the Buddha arrives, and before he teaches anything, he asks them a question. Is there a teacher here you trust? And the villagers say, honestly: no. They've heard too many confident voices. What would you say to a village like that? Today, the answer in the sixtieth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings.
screen: `A VILLAGE CALLED SĀLĀ.` → `TOO MANY CONFIDENT VOICES.` → `IS THERE A TEACHER YOU TRUST? NO.`

segments.voice: He doesn't try to out-argue the other teachers. He offers what the sutta calls apaṇṇaka, a teaching that's sure, that can't go wrong. Here's how it works. Take two people. The first holds that there is no other world, that giving bears no fruit, that good and bad actions have no results. So he lives carelessly with his body, his speech and his mind. The second holds that actions do have results, and lives carefully. Now, says the Buddha, suppose the first person is right, and there is no other world. Even then, the careless one is called a person of bad conduct by the wise, here and now. And if there is another world, he loses twice. The careful one? If there's no other world, the wise still praise her here and now. If there is, she gains there too. The sutta borrows a word from dice. She has made the winning throw, and it wins both ways. Notice what he doesn't ask for. He doesn't say: believe in rebirth first, and then be good. He says the question can stay open, and the way to live comes out the same. That's why we call it the safe bet. Buddhist traditions teach rebirth, and this sutta also speaks to the listener who isn't sure yet. It asks one thing of the listener: live as if what you do has results. On an ordinary Tuesday, that might mean telling the truth on a form nobody checks. You don't have to settle the universe first. The bet pays in this life, and it pays again if there's another.
screen: `APAṆṆAKA: A TEACHING THAT CAN'T GO WRONG.` · `TWO PEOPLE, TWO VIEWS.` · `IF THERE'S NO NEXT WORLD, STILL PRAISED.` · `THE WINNING THROW, BOTH WAYS.` · then, large: `THE SAFE BET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: live the safe bet today. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one choice waiting for you later: a message, a purchase, a conversation. Ask it two questions, slowly. If nothing I do echoes past today, is this worth doing well? And if it does echo, further than I can see? Let the answers arrive on the out-breath. Notice whether they point the same way. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
The safe bet. Live as though actions have results, and you come out ahead whether or not there is another world. Today's word.
Your line: the safe bet. Today, make one choice you'd be glad of either way, whether this life is all there is or not. Day four hundred fifty-two.

he leaves the question open: the bet comes out ahead either way.
the careful person gains even if there is no other world

the sutta borrows its image from a game of dice
the careful one has made the winning throw, and it wins both ways.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha, arriving at Sālā. the villagers say they trust no teacher. what do you offer them?
options: a sharper argument than the last teacher's
a way to live that comes out ahead whoever is right
a demand that they choose a side today
fork.reveal: he offers apaṇṇaka, the sure teaching: live as though actions have results, and you lose nothing either way.

original.note: Pali apaṇṇaka: sure, beyond dispute. it is the title of this sutta, and of the first tale in the Jataka collection.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bet is a gamble.
what it means: a way of living that comes out ahead however the big question falls.
what a scholar hears: apaṇṇaka, 'incontrovertible', with the dice words kaṭaggaha and kaliggaha for the winning and losing throw; the Jataka collection opens with a tale of the same name.

453.title: Before, during, after
453.hook: to Rahula: reflect before, during and after every act of body, speech and mind
453.howItsDone: In many Theravada communities this sutta is among the first taught to novices, and monks and nuns regularly acknowledge their faults to one another before the fortnightly recitation of the monastic rules.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the safe bet. Live as though actions have results, and you lose nothing either way. Which choice did you make that you'd be glad of either way? Day four hundred fifty-three.

A small boy sets out a seat and a basin of water. His father is coming to visit, and his father is the Buddha. The boy is Rāhula, and tradition says he's about seven. The Buddha washes his feet, and leaves a little water in the bottom of the basin. Rāhula, do you see this little bit of water? Yes. That's how little of a monk's life is left, he says, in anyone who isn't ashamed to tell a deliberate lie. He tips the water out, turns the basin upside down, then turns it back, empty. A lesson a child can see. And then he hands his son a mirror.
screen: `A SEAT AND A BASIN OF WATER.` → `A LITTLE WATER LEFT.` → `TIPPED OUT. TURNED OVER. EMPTY.`

segments.voice: Not a real one. A question. What is a mirror for, Rāhula? For reflecting, the boy says. The Pali word is paccavekkhaṇa, looking back at, looking over. So, says the Buddha, an action should be done after reflecting, again and again. That's the heart of the sutta, the sixty-first in the Middle-Length Sayings, and it's built in threes. Three kinds of action: body, speech and mind. Three moments: before, during and after. And one question, asked each time: will this lead to harm for me, for others, or for both? Before you act, ask it. If the answer is harm, don't do it. If it's harmless and good, go ahead. While you're acting, ask again, because things change halfway through a sentence. If it's turning harmful, stop. And afterward, look back. If it caused harm, the Buddha tells Rāhula, go and tell a teacher or a wise companion, and be careful next time. If it did good, he says, let yourself be glad, and keep training. Notice two things. First, the boy isn't told to feel terrible. He's told to see clearly, to say it to someone, and to begin again. Second, the mind is included. You can't confess a passing thought to anyone, so for the mind the sutta says: be troubled by it, turn from it, and go on. Monks and nuns in some communities still say what went wrong to one another, regularly, out loud. It's the same mirror, held up together. The word today is the first of the three: before. It's the cheapest moment to change anything.
screen: `WHAT IS A MIRROR FOR?` · `BODY, SPEECH AND MIND.` · `HARM TO ME, TO OTHERS, TO BOTH?` · `IF IT HARMED, SAY SO, AND BEGIN AGAIN.` · then, large: `BEFORE, DURING, AFTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reflect three times on one act. Settle, and choose one small thing you'll do soon, like sending a reply or speaking to someone at home. Before: picture it, and ask whether it could hurt you, them, or both. During: imagine yourself halfway through, and notice where you might need to stop. After: picture it done, and see how you'd want to look back on it. One breath for each. Then just breathe. The bell holds the time.
Before. The first of three looks the Buddha taught his son: before, during and after every act of body, speech and mind. Today's word.
Your line: before, during, after. Today, pick one conversation and hold up the mirror three times: before you start, in the middle, and once it's over. Day four hundred fifty-three.

before, during and after: three looks for every act.

stop there

fork.reveal: the look 'during' is there for exactly this: if an act is turning harmful while you do it, the Buddha tells Rāhula to stop.

original.note: Pali paccavekkhaṇa: reflecting, looking back over. the Buddha's answer to what a mirror is for.

trapdoor: what you thought: before means think before you speak.
what it means: one of three looks, before, during and after, at every act of body, speech and mind.
what a scholar hears: MN 61, the Ambalaṭṭhikā Rāhulovāda Sutta; its key term paccavekkhaṇa, 'reviewing', returns throughout the Pali texts on monastic training.

454.title: Be like the earth
454.hook: to Rahula: be like earth, water, fire, wind and space, which don't recoil from what is thrown on them
454.howItsDone: Some Buddhist meditation teachers use the elements, especially the earth, as images for a steady mind; this sutta sets them beside the four immeasurables and mindfulness of breathing.

segments.voice: Yesterday: before, the first of three looks the Buddha taught his young son. Your line was before, during, after. Did you hold up the mirror in one conversation? Day four hundred fifty-four.

Rāhula is older now. The commentaries say eighteen. He's walking behind his father on the morning alms round, admiring, the commentaries add, how alike the two of them look. The Buddha looks back at him and says something sharp about the body: whatever form there is, past, future or present, should be seen as not mine, not I, not my self. Rāhula turns back, skips the meal, and sits under a tree. Sāriputta finds him there and tells him to develop mindfulness of breathing. That evening Rāhula goes to his father to ask about it, and the answer begins somewhere else. Not with what he is. With what to be like.
screen: `THE ALMS ROUND, AT EIGHTEEN.` → `ADMIRING HIMSELF.` → `HE TURNS BACK AND SITS DOWN.`

segments.voice: Rāhula, develop a meditation that is like the earth. That's how the sixty-second sutta of the Middle-Length Sayings begins its answer. People throw all sorts of things on the earth, the Buddha says. Clean things and filthy ones: excrement, urine, spit, pus and blood. The earth isn't horrified or humiliated by any of it. It doesn't recoil. In the same way, when pleasant and unpleasant contacts land on you, they won't take over your mind. Then he goes on, element by element. Be like water. People wash clean and dirty things in water, and it isn't disgusted. Be like fire, which burns clean and dirty things alike. Be like the wind, which blows over all of them. And be like space, which isn't established anywhere at all. It's a teaching about receiving. Not about becoming hard like a rock; the earth in this picture isn't armored. It's wide. Things land, and there's room for them. Praise lands. An insult in a group chat lands. A spilled drink on your shirt before a meeting lands. The earth doesn't pretend nothing fell. It just isn't knocked off balance. After the elements, the sutta keeps going: loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy and equanimity, then more, ending with sixteen steps of breathing. But the elements come first, almost as a foundation. A Dhammapada verse, in Max Müller's words, says of the one who does his duty that he "is tolerant like the earth." The steadiness isn't coldness. It's a kind of hospitality.
screen: `A MEDITATION LIKE THE EARTH.` · `IT DOESN'T RECOIL.` · `WATER, FIRE, WIND AND SPACE.` · `NOT HARD. WIDE.` · then, large: `BE LIKE THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be like the earth for an hour. Start now, sitting. Feel the weight of your body resting on the chair or the floor, and the ground under that, holding everything without complaint. As sounds come, let them land. As thoughts come, pleasant or not, let them land too, without pushing them off. You're the ground they fall on. After the bell, carry that for the next hour, and notice what lands. The bell holds the time.
Be like the earth. People throw clean and dirty things on the earth, and it doesn't recoil. The Buddha's advice to his son for meeting whatever comes. Today's word.
Your line: be like the earth. For one hour today, let whatever lands on you land, praise or complaint, and see if you can stay wide. Day four hundred fifty-four.

the Buddha looks back and speaks about form, and Rāhula turns back to sit under a tree.

fork.setup: someone throws an insult at you in front of others. in the earth teaching, what's the earth's answer?
options: throw it back
pretend it didn't happen
let it land without being knocked off balance
fork.reveal: the earth isn't horrified or humiliated by what falls on it, and doesn't pretend nothing fell. it stays steady.

original.note: Pali pathavī: earth. the sutta's phrase is a meditation 'like the earth'.

trapdoor: what you thought: be like the earth means be grounded.
what it means: let pleasant and unpleasant contacts land without recoiling, the way the earth takes what is thrown on it.
what a scholar hears: MN 62, the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, runs from the elements through the four immeasurables to sixteen steps of breathing, a whole meditation program in one discourse.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)

455.title: The undeclared
455.hook: ten questions the Buddha set aside, and why silence was the answer
455.howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers tell the parable of the poisoned arrow to students who want metaphysical questions settled first, and the ten undeclared questions come up in commentaries and debates across schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha told his son: be like the earth, which doesn't recoil from what's thrown on it. What landed on you, and did you stay wide? Day four hundred fifty-five, the end of a week.

A monk named Māluṅkyāputta is sitting alone, and he's had enough. There are questions the Buddha never answers. Is the world eternal, or not? Is it finite, or infinite? Are the soul and the body the same thing, or different? Does an awakened one exist after death, or not, or both, or neither? Ten questions in all. So he goes to the Buddha with an ultimatum: answer them, or I'm giving up the training and going home. It's the kind of message you type at 2am. Today, what the Buddha says back.
screen: `TEN QUESTIONS.` → `ANSWER THEM, OR I LEAVE.` → `AN ULTIMATUM.`

segments.voice: First, he asks Māluṅkyāputta a question of his own. Did I ever promise you, come and train with me and I'll answer these? No. Did you ever say, I'll train only if you do? No. Then, he says, who are you, and what are you walking away from? And then comes a picture. Suppose, the Buddha says, a man is shot with an arrow thickly smeared with poison. His friends bring a surgeon. And the man says: don't pull it out until I know who shot me. Was he a noble, a brahmin, a merchant, a laborer? What was his name, his clan? Was he tall or short, dark or fair? What village was he from? What kind of bow was it? What was the string made of, and the feathers on the shaft? That man, the Buddha says, would die before he ever found out. So the ten questions stay undeclared, avyākata, not answered either way. Why? Not because they're forbidden, and the sutta doesn't call them meaningless. Because answering them isn't beneficial, he says. It doesn't lead to letting go, to peace, to awakening. And what has he declared? This is suffering. This is its arising. This is its ending. This is the way. Four things, all about pulling the arrow out. The sutta ends with a line worth keeping: remember what I've left undeclared as undeclared, and what I've declared as declared. Buddhist schools have gone on discussing the ten questions. But the silence itself is a teaching. Some questions you can carry for a lifetime without letting them stop you walking.
screen: `DID I EVER PROMISE YOU THAT?` · `THE POISONED ARROW.` · `NOT BENEFICIAL, NOT LEADING TO PEACE.` · `FOUR THINGS DECLARED.` · then, large: `THE UNDECLARED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave one question unanswered. Settle and breathe. Let one big question come up, one you've chewed on: why something happened, what comes after, whether you chose right. Name it once, gently. Then, instead of answering, set it down beside you like a closed book. Return to the breath. When the question taps your shoulder, notice it, and come back. It can stay undeclared for now. The bell holds the time.
The undeclared. Ten questions the Buddha set aside, because answering them doesn't pull the arrow out. Today's word.

Your line: the undeclared. Today, let one question stay open and do the next useful thing anyway. And that's week sixty-five: the dog-duty ascetic, the trap question, how many feelings, the safe bet, before, the earth, and the undeclared. Day four hundred fifty-five.
